planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; this clump-forming woodland sedge establishes slowly and resents being disturbed once settled.

directions: Native to woodland margins in southern China, this clump-forming sedge is grown less for its foliage than for its unusual flowering habit, sending up slender stalks topped with bright rose-pink to magenta flower spikes in late summer and fall that stand out sharply against the glossy, dark green, strap-shaped leaves below. Plant divisions in part to full shade and evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, siting it where winter wet will not sit around the crown in the coldest end of its range. It forms a tidy, non-running clump rather than spreading aggressively, making it a well-behaved companion for hostas, ferns, and other woodland perennials in a shaded border. In regions colder than the lower end of its hardiness range, a protective winter mulch helps the evergreen foliage come through cleanly.

planting.note: Install divisions or plugs in spring along streambanks, pond margins, or rain gardens in consistently moist to wet soil; it spreads by rhizomes to form dense colonies over time.

directions: This robust evergreen sedge is native to wet forests, streambanks, and tidal marsh edges from British Columbia to central California, where it forms large, arching clumps of glossy, dark green foliage under a partial canopy. It spreads steadily by rhizomes in consistently moist to saturated soil, making it a workhorse choice for rain gardens, bioswales, and pond margins that need erosion control along with wildlife habitat. While it tolerates full sun where soil stays wet year-round, foliage color and texture are often best in the partial shade of streamside alders and conifers that mirror its native habitat. Established clumps need little care beyond an occasional thinning to keep colonies from crowding smaller companion plants.

planting.note: Install plugs on close spacing in spring or fall in part shade to full sun; rhizomes knit plugs together into a solid sod within one to two growing seasons.

directions: Found along streambanks and in valley grasslands throughout California, this rhizomatous native sedge forms a fine-textured, deep green sod that tolerates considerably more shade than the drier-site Carex pansa and Carex praegracilis typically used for sedge lawns. It spreads readily by rhizomes to knit together into a dense, mowable turf substitute, or it can be left unmowed as a soft meadow with gently arching foliage. Once established along a shaded streamside or beneath high tree canopy, it needs only occasional irrigation to stay green through the dry California summer. Its shade tolerance makes it a go-to choice for no-mow lawn conversions in wooded yards where full-sun sedge lawns would thin out.
sources: UC Davis Arboretum and Public Garden

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in rich, moist woodland soil in partial to full shade; it forms neat, non-aggressive tufts rather than spreading far.

directions: This fine-leaved woodland sedge grows wild in moist, shaded forests across a broad swath of temperate North America, from the Appalachians and upper Midwest to mountain forests of the Pacific Coast. It forms loose, airy tufts of soft green foliage topped by slender, drooping seed spikes in late spring, blending unobtrusively into a shaded native plant palette rather than standing out as a specimen. Because it clumps rather than spreading by rhizomes, it mixes well in tight plantings among wildflowers, ferns, and other woodland sedges without crowding its neighbors. Give it consistent moisture and leaf-litter-rich soil to mimic the forest floor conditions where it naturally thrives.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
